# Chasing the Pattern to Its Limit

<!-- STEP id="the-carpet" -->
Push a ball across a thick carpet. It grips hard — lots of friction — and the ball stops almost immediately.

<!-- STEP id="the-tiles" -->
Push it the same way across smooth floor tiles instead. Less friction, less opposing force — and the ball rolls noticeably farther before it stops.

<!-- STEP id="the-ice" -->
Push it across wet ice — next to no friction at all. It glides almost the length of the room, barely losing speed the whole way.

<!-- STEP id="spot-the-pattern" -->
Every time the opposing force gets smaller, the ball keeps its velocity for longer and travels farther before stopping.

<!-- STEP id="the-leap" -->
Now follow that pattern all the way to its limit: what if the opposing force could shrink to exactly zero? Distance traveled would keep growing without any limit — the ball would never stop on its own. It would carry on at the same velocity forever.

<!-- STEP id="naming-the-leap" -->
No real surface on Earth is ever perfectly frictionless — there's always some carpet, tile, ice, or air resistance getting in the way, so this exact case can't be built in a lab. But the pattern never breaks, however far you push it. That leap — trusting a clean pattern past the point you can actually test it — is what led Galileo, and later Newton, to the law you're about to meet.
